title: Calculus I: limits, derivatives and an introduction to the integral
summary: A first university course in single-variable calculus. Students study limits and continuity, derivative rules, and applications such as related rates, optimization and curve sketching. The course ends with an introduction to the definite integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
brief: Calculus I for first-year undergraduates: a 15-week semester, three 50-minute lectures a week and one 50-minute recitation led by a teaching assistant. Limits and continuity, derivatives and their rules, applications of the derivative (related rates, optimization, curve sketching), and an introduction to the integral. Textbook: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals. Weekly online homework 15%, weekly recitation quizzes 15%, two midterms 20% each, final exam 30%.
setup: Recitation is led by a teaching assistant

segments.title: How fast is fast at one instant?
segments.description:
Put the speedometer question on the screen.
Everyone writes one or two sentences alone for two minutes.
Students compare with a neighbor for two minutes, then two or three share.
Gather the idea that speed over a shrinking time window settles toward a number.
segments.teacherNotes: Likely answers: the car would cover 80 miles if it held this speed for an hour; or its speed over a very short window. Both are good. The second is the route to the derivative.
shown: A speedometer reads 80 mph at 2:15 pm. Speed is distance divided by time, and an instant lasts no time. What does the speedometer reading mean? Write one or two sentences.

segments.title: The tangent problem
segments.description:
Pose the problem: find the tangent line to y = x² at P(1, 1). A tangent has no slope formula yet, so approximate it with secants.
Draw secants through P and Q(x, x²) and write m = (x² − 1)/(x − 1).
Students compute m for x = 2 and x = 1.5, then predict the slopes for x = 1.1 and x = 1.01 before the table is completed.
Complete the table, read off the slope 2, and write the tangent line.
segments.teacherNotes: Table: x = 2 gives 3; 1.5 gives 2.5; 1.1 gives 2.1; 1.01 gives 2.01; 0.99 gives 1.99; 0.9 gives 1.9. Tangent: y = 2x − 1. Say this is an estimate; limits will make it exact.
shown: Find the tangent line to y = x² at P(1, 1).
Secant through P(1, 1) and Q(x, x²): m = (x² − 1)/(x − 1)

segments.title: Secant slopes at P(2, 4)
segments.description:
Students work alone on y = x² at P(2, 4) for eight minutes. They compute secant slopes for x = 3, 2.5, 2.1, 2.01 and 1.99, estimate the tangent slope and write the tangent line.
Partners compare for two minutes.
The instructor works the solution on the board for four minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Slopes: 5, 4.5, 4.1, 4.01, 3.99. Estimate 4. Tangent: y − 4 = 4(x − 2), so y = 4x − 4. Some will see m = x + 2; welcome it, do not require it. Common slip: using x instead of x − 2 in the denominator.
shown: For y = x² at P(2, 4), find the slope of the secant through Q(x, x²) for x = 3, 2.5, 2.1, 2.01, 1.99. Estimate the slope of the tangent at P and write its equation.

segments.title: Tangent lines from secant lines
segments.description:
Students write one sentence on how the tangent slope at a point can be found from secant slopes, two minutes.
Two or three read theirs aloud, two minutes.
Preview the second lecture: the same idea applied to a falling ball and its velocity.
segments.teacherNotes: Good answer: the tangent slope is the number secant slopes approach as the second point moves toward P. Listen for ‘from both sides’.

segments.title: How far has the ball fallen?
segments.description:
The screen gives s(1) = 4.9 m. Students compute s(2) and the average velocity from t = 1 to t = 2 alone for three minutes.
They compare with a neighbor for one minute.
Write average velocity = (change in position)/(change in time) and confirm 14.7 m/s with the class, one minute.
segments.teacherNotes: s(2) = 19.6 m, average velocity 14.7 m/s. The formula 4.9t² is free fall near Earth, half of g = 9.8 m/s² times t².
shown: A ball is dropped. After t seconds it has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters, so s(1) = 4.9 m. Find s(2) and the average velocity from t = 1 to t = 2.

segments.title: The velocity problem
segments.description:
Pose the problem: a ball is dropped from an observation deck 450 m above the ground, s(t) = 4.9t². How fast is it falling at t = 5?
Students compute s(5) and the average velocity over [5, 6] for three minutes.
Shrink the interval to [5, 5.1], [5, 5.05], [5, 5.01] and [5, 5.001]; students predict each value before it is shown.
Simplify (s(5 + h) − s(5))/h to 49 + 4.9h and read off 49 m/s.
segments.teacherNotes: s(5) = 122.5 m. Averages: 53.9, 49.49, 49.245, 49.049, 49.0049 m/s. Say ‘approaches 49', never ‘equals 49 when h = 0'. The ball lands after about 9.6 s, so t = 5 is in flight.
shown: A ball is dropped from a deck 450 m above the ground. Position after t seconds: s(t) = 4.9t² meters.
Average velocity over [5, 5 + h] = (s(5 + h) − s(5))/h

segments.title: A stone dropped from a bridge
segments.description:
With the same position function, each student finds the average velocity over [2, 3], [2, 2.5], [2, 2.1] and [2, 2.01] and estimates the velocity at t = 2.
Students work alone for six minutes, then partners check each other for two minutes.
The instructor shows the table for two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: s(2) = 19.6. Averages: 24.5, 22.05, 20.09, 19.649 m/s; estimate 19.6 m/s (the quotient is 19.6 + 4.9h). Common error: dividing by the endpoint t instead of the interval length.

segments.title: One calculation behind two problems
segments.description:
Put the secant slope and the average velocity side by side. Both are a change in output over a change in input.
Write the common form (f(a + h) − f(a))/h and name it a difference quotient.
Say tangent slope and instantaneous velocity are what this quotient settles toward as h shrinks.
Students tell a partner in one sentence what ‘settles toward’ should mean, two minutes, and two are heard.
segments.teacherNotes: On the position graph, secant slope is average velocity and tangent slope is instantaneous velocity. Allow h < 0 too: [4.9, 5] gives values just below 49.

segments.title: Find the mistake
segments.description:
Everyone reads the student’s solution and writes what is wrong and a corrected answer, four minutes.
Pairs compare for three minutes.
Two pairs report and the class agrees on the correction.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistake: 0/0 is undefined, not 0, and h = 0 gives no information. Fix: for h ≠ 0 the quotient is 19.6 + 4.9h, whose values approach 19.6 m/s. The ball is moving at t = 2.

segments.title: Two problems, one limit idea
segments.description:
Summarize: tangent slope and instantaneous velocity are both what a difference quotient approaches.
Tell students the third lecture gives ‘approaches’ a precise meaning.

segments.title: A function that is undefined at 3
segments.description:
The screen gives f(3) as undefined and f(3.1) = 6.1. Students compute f(2.9) alone for two minutes.
They compare with a neighbor for one minute.
Students predict f(2.99) and f(3.01) with their neighbor, two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: f(3) is 0/0, undefined. f(2.9) = 5.9 and f(3.1) = 6.1; f(2.99) = 5.99 and f(3.01) = 6.01, so values head toward 6. Away from 3 the function equals x + 3.
shown: f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3). f(3) is undefined (0/0), and f(3.1) = 6.1. Compute f(2.9).

segments.title: What a limit says
segments.description:
Write the informal definition: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) gets as close to L as we like when x is taken close enough to a, with x ≠ a.
Estimate lim_{x→1} (x − 1)/(x² − 1) from a table. Students compute g(0.9) and g(1.1) first, then more rows are shown.
Point out that g(1) is undefined yet the limit is 0.5.
Students tell a partner why f(a) plays no role, one minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Left: 0.5 gives 0.66667; 0.9 gives 0.52632; 0.99 gives 0.50251; 0.999 gives 0.50025. Right: 1.5 gives 0.4; 1.1 gives 0.47619; 1.01 gives 0.49751; 1.001 gives 0.49975. Limit 1/2. Common error: thinking x must reach a.

segments.title: Limits from graphs, and when tables mislead
segments.description:
Show the graph of f: the line y = x + 1 with an open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot at (2, 1). Students write lim_{x→2} f(x) and f(2) alone, then compare.
Show a graph that follows y = x + 1 for x < 1 and sits at y = 3 for x ≥ 1. Students decide whether the values approach one number.
Show sin(π/x) at x = 1, 1/2, 1/3 and then at x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13; students say why the table never settles.
segments.teacherNotes: First graph: limit 3, f(2) = 1. Second: from the left values approach 2, from the right they equal 3, so the limit does not exist. sin(π/x) gives 0 at x = 1/n and 1 at x = 2/(4n + 1), however close to 0.
shown: Graph 1: the line y = x + 1 for x ≠ 2, open circle at (2, 3), filled dot at (2, 1).
Graph 2: y = x + 1 for x < 1 (open circle at (1, 2)), and y = 3 for x ≥ 1 (filled dot at (1, 3)).

segments.title: Estimate four limits
segments.description:
Students estimate each limit from the table or graph shown, alone for eight minutes.
Pairs compare and settle disagreements, two minutes.
The instructor goes through each item and asks which need both sides.

segments.title: Say it in words, then build examples
segments.description:
Students work alone for five minutes. They write in their own words what lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means, then sketch one function with lim_{x→2} f(x) = 3 and f(2) = 5, marking open circles and filled dots, with a sentence on why it fits.
Partners swap papers and check each against the meaning of a limit, two minutes.
Three students share and the class judges.
segments.teacherNotes: Good wording: f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close to a, x ≠ a. Watch for ‘f(x) reaches L’ or ‘x = a’. Sketch: open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot at (2, 5). The sentence should say the values near x = 2 head toward 3 while f(2) is 5.

segments.title: What the problem session holds
segments.description:
Summarize: limits are estimated from tables and graphs, and f(a) does not decide the limit.
Tell students the problem session works problems on all three lectures and holds a Weekly recitation quiz.

The teaching assistant explains that students try each problem first and solutions are worked afterwards.

The assistant gives the instructor’s announcement of what students may bring.

segments.title: Tangent to y = 1/x at P(2, 1/2)
segments.description:
Pairs compute the secant slopes for x = 3, 2.5, 2.1, 2.01 and estimate the tangent slope, five minutes.
One pair gives its four slopes and estimate, one minute.
The assistant works the solution on the board and writes the tangent line, four minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Slopes: −0.1667, −0.2, −0.2381, −0.2488; estimate −0.25. Each slope equals −1/(2x). Tangent: y = −x/4 + 1. Common slip: a sign error in 1/x − 1/2.
shown: Find the slope of the tangent to y = 1/x at P(2, 1/2). Compute the slopes of the secants through Q at x = 3, 2.5, 2.1, 2.01.

segments.title: Velocity of an object dropped on the Moon
segments.description:
Students work alone for five minutes on the Moon problem.
The assistant works the solution for three minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: s(4) = 12.96 m. Averages: 6.561 and 6.4881 m/s. The quotient is 6.48 + 0.81h, so the estimate is 6.48 m/s. The constant 0.81 is half of the Moon’s g, 1.62 m/s².

segments.title: Estimate lim (sin x)/x
segments.description:
Students estimate the limit from the table and write one sentence of justification, three minutes.
They compare with a partner for two minutes.
The assistant takes two answers and works the reasoning on the board, three minutes.
segments.teacherNotes: Limit 1. Values rise toward 1 from both sides, and (sin x)/x is undefined at 0. The table is evidence for an estimate, not a proof.

segments.title: Recitation quiz
segments.description:
Clear the board and screen of earlier work.
The assistant gives out the recitation quiz and students answer its questions.
It is marked in points out of 12.
segments.teacherNotes:
Questions, answers and points (12 in all):
Q1 (4 points). A rock is dropped from a cliff and has fallen s(t) = 16t² feet after t seconds. Find the average velocity over [3, 3.1] and over [3, 3.01]. Estimate the velocity at t = 3, with units. Answer: s(3) = 144; 97.6 ft/s (1 point); 96.16 ft/s (1 point); estimate 96 ft/s (1 point); units ft/s (1 point).
Q2 (3 points). For f(x) = (eˣ − 1)/x: x = −0.1 gives 0.9516; −0.01 gives 0.9950; 0.01 gives 1.0050; 0.1 gives 1.0517. Estimate lim_{x→0} f(x) and say what in the table supports it. Answer: 1 (2 points); values from both sides move toward 1 (1 point).
Q3 (3 points). The graph of g is the line through (0, 3) and (2, 5), with an open circle at (1, 4) and a filled dot at (1, 1). Find lim_{x→1} g(x) and g(1), and say whether they must be equal. Answer: 4 (1 point); 1 (1 point); no, the limit does not depend on the value at 1 (1 point).
Q4 (2 points). Explain in words what lim_{x→4} f(x) = 7 means. Does it tell you f(4) = 7? Answer: f(x) can be made as close to 7 as we like by taking x close to 4, x ≠ 4 (1 point); no, f(4) may differ or be undefined (1 point).

segments.title: Homework and what comes next
segments.description:
Set the Weekly online homework (15%), due at the first meeting of the lesson ‘Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits’ and submitted online before it.
Tell students to read Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, section 2.3, Calculating Limits Using the Limit Laws, before that meeting.
Next time students compute limits with the limit laws, factoring and the Squeeze Theorem and read one-sided and infinite limits. The Weekly recitation quizzes quiz at that lesson’s problem session covers this, and the instructor announces what to bring.
A practice quiz on this lesson is for after class and counts toward no grade.
Before students leave, tell them that next time they sit “Weekly recitation quizzes: Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits”, and what it covers.

keyIdeas: The slope of the tangent line at a point P is the number that the slopes of secant lines through P settle toward as the second point moves toward P.
Instantaneous velocity is the number that average velocities over shorter and shorter time intervals settle toward. It comes from the same calculation as the tangent slope.
lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a. The value f(a) plays no role.
Tables and graphs give estimates of a limit, and a table can mislead: values of sin(π/x) near 0 never settle.

vocabulary.definition: A line through two points on a curve. Its slope is the average rate of change between them.
The line through a point on a curve whose slope is the limit of the secant slopes as the second point approaches that point.
A function s(t) giving an object’s location at time t, such as s(t) = 4.9t² meters for a dropped ball.
The change in position divided by the change in time over an interval.
The number that average velocities approach as the time interval shrinks to zero length.
The expression (f(a + h) − f(a))/h, the slope of the secant through x = a and x = a + h.
The number L that f(x) approaches as x approaches a, written lim_{x→a} f(x) = L. It does not depend on f(a).
A limit does not exist when f(x) does not approach a single number, for example when the two sides approach different numbers or the values oscillate.

study.overview: This lesson introduced two questions that look different: how steep is a curve at one point, and how fast is an object moving at one instant. Both are answered the same way. You compute an average over a small interval, shrink the interval, and ask what number the averages settle toward. That idea is a limit. Review it in Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, sections 2.1 and 2.2 (to confirm).

points.heading: The tangent slope is what secant slopes settle toward
points.explanation: A tangent line has no slope formula yet, but a secant line through two points does. Take y = x² and P(1, 1). For a second point Q(x, x²), the secant slope is m = (x² − 1)/(x − 1). Then x = 2 gives 3, x = 1.5 gives 2.5, x = 1.1 gives 2.1 and x = 1.01 gives 2.01. From the other side, x = 0.9 gives 1.9 and x = 0.99 gives 1.99. The slopes from both sides head toward 2, so the tangent slope at P is estimated as 2. The tangent line is y − 1 = 2(x − 1), or y = 2x − 1. This is an estimate from a table. Limits will later make it exact. Check that you approach P from both sides, not just one.

points.heading: Instantaneous velocity comes from the same calculation
points.explanation: Suppose a ball is dropped and has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters after t seconds. Average velocity is the change in position divided by the change in time. To find the velocity at t = 5, start with s(5) = 122.5 m and compute (s(5 + h) − s(5))/h over shorter intervals. Over [5, 6] it is 53.9 m/s. Over [5, 5.1] it is 49.49 m/s. Over [5, 5.05] it is 49.245 m/s, over [5, 5.01] it is 49.049 m/s and over [5, 5.001] it is 49.0049 m/s. Algebra shows the quotient equals 49 + 4.9h for every h ≠ 0. As h shrinks, the averages approach 49 m/s. Say ‘approaches 49', not ‘equals 49 when h = 0'. Putting h = 0 gives 0/0, which is undefined and tells you nothing. The expression (f(a + h) − f(a))/h is called a difference quotient. It is the secant slope on a graph and the average velocity on a position function. Tangent slope and instantaneous velocity are what it approaches as h shrinks.

points.heading: What a limit means, and why f(a) does not matter
points.explanation: The statement lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means that f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a. The value f(a) plays no role, and f(a) may not even exist. Take f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3). At x = 3 it gives 0/0, so f(3) is undefined. But f(2.9) = 5.9, f(2.99) = 5.99, f(3.01) = 6.01 and f(3.1) = 6.1. The values head toward 6, so lim_{x→3} f(x) = 6. For x ≠ 3 the function equals x + 3, which explains the pattern. A common error is to think x must reach a. The limit describes what happens near a, not at a.

points.heading: Tables and graphs give estimates, and a table can mislead
points.explanation: A limit estimate needs values from both sides of a. On a graph, an open circle at (2, 3) with a filled dot at (2, 1) on the line y = x + 1 means the limit is 3 while the function value is 1. Now take a graph that follows y = x + 1 for x < 1 and sits at y = 3 for x ≥ 1. From the left the values approach 2. From the right they are 3. No single number is approached from both sides, so the limit does not exist. A table can also hide the behavior. For f(x) = sin(π/x), the points x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 all give 0, which suggests a limit of 0. The points x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13 all give 1. In fact f is 0 at x = 1/n and 1 at x = 2/(4n + 1), however close to 0 you look, so the values never settle. A table is evidence for an estimate, not a proof.

handouts.title: A stone dropped from a bridge
handouts.usedIn: A stone dropped from a bridge

blocks.text: A stone is dropped from a bridge. After t seconds it has fallen s(t) = 4.9t² meters. Work alone. Find the average velocity over each interval, then estimate the velocity at t = 2.

blocks.hint: Your estimate of the velocity at t = 2, with units, and the working that supports it.

handouts.key:
Average velocity over [2, b] is (s(b) − s(2))/(b − 2), with s(2) = 4.9(2²) = 19.6 m.

[2, 3]: s(3) = 44.1 m; (44.1 − 19.6)/(3 − 2) = 24.5 m/s.
[2, 2.5]: s(2.5) = 30.625 m; (30.625 − 19.6)/0.5 = 22.05 m/s.
[2, 2.1]: s(2.1) = 21.609 m; (21.609 − 19.6)/0.1 = 20.09 m/s.
[2, 2.01]: s(2.01) = 19.79649 m; (19.79649 − 19.6)/0.01 = 19.649 m/s.

Estimate at t = 2: 19.6 m/s downward. For h ≠ 0, (s(2 + h) − s(2))/h = (19.6h + 4.9h²)/h = 19.6 + 4.9h. These averages approach 19.6 as h approaches 0.

Look for division by the interval length and an estimate supported by the shrinking intervals. Common slip: dividing by the endpoint rather than by the change in time.

handouts.title: Find the mistake

blocks.text: Read the solution below. It contains a mistake. Say what is wrong, then give a corrected answer.
Problem
A stone is dropped from a bridge, and s(t) = 4.9t² meters after t seconds. Find its velocity at t = 2.
A student's solution

items: The average velocity over [2, 2 + h] is (s(2 + h) − s(2))/h.
So the velocity at t = 2 is 0 m/s. The stone is not moving yet.

blocks.hint: What is wrong with this solution?
Write a corrected answer for the velocity at t = 2, with your working.

handouts.key:
What is wrong: 0/0 is undefined. Substituting h = 0 does not give a velocity of 0. The difference quotient must be evaluated for h ≠ 0, and its behavior as h approaches 0 determines the instantaneous velocity.

Corrected answer: s(2) = 19.6 m. Expanding gives 4.9(2 + h)² − 19.6 = 19.6h + 4.9h². For h ≠ 0, (s(2 + h) − s(2))/h = 19.6 + 4.9h. As h approaches 0, this approaches 19.6. The velocity at t = 2 is 19.6 m/s downward.

Look for a distinction between taking a limit and substituting h = 0. Common slip: treating an undefined quotient as zero.

handouts.title: Estimate four limits

blocks.text: Estimate each limit from the table or the description given. Work alone, then compare with a partner.
1. lim x→2 of (x² − 4)/(x − 2)

blocks.hint: Your estimate of the limit.
Your estimate of the limit.

blocks.text: 3. lim x→3 of f(x)
The graph of f is the line y = 2x at every x except x = 3. There is an open circle at (3, 6) and a filled dot at (3, 1). Find lim x→3 of f(x) and f(3).

blocks.hint: The limit and f(3).

blocks.text: 4. lim x→0 of h(x), where h(x) = |x|/x

blocks.hint: Your estimate of the limit, or a statement that it does not exist, with a reason.

handouts.key:
1. The estimated limit is 4. From the left, 3.9, 3.99 and 3.999 approach 4; from the right, 4.1, 4.01 and 4.001 approach 4. For x ≠ 2, (x² − 4)/(x − 2) = x + 2. Common slip: concluding that the limit does not exist because the expression is undefined at x = 2.

2. The estimated limit is 0.25. Values from both sides approach 0.25. For x ≠ 0, rationalizing gives (√(x + 4) − 2)/x = 1/(√(x + 4) + 2), which approaches 1/4. Common slip: interpreting 0/0 as the limit.

3. lim_{x→3} f(x) = 6; f(3) = 1. The line approaches the open circle at (3, 6) from both sides. The filled dot at (3, 1) gives the function value. Common slip: using the filled dot to determine the limit.

4. The limit does not exist. For negative x, |x|/x = −1; for positive x, |x|/x = 1. The two sides approach different values. Look for an explicit comparison of both sides. Common slip: averaging −1 and 1 to claim a limit of 0.

handouts.title: Say it in words, then build examples
handouts.usedIn: Say it in words, then build examples

blocks.text: Work alone. Your partner will check your answers against the meaning of a limit.

blocks.hint: In your own words, what does lim x→a of f(x) = L mean?
Sketch a function f with lim x→2 of f(x) = 3 and f(2) = 5. Mark any open circles and filled dots, and add a sentence saying why it fits.

handouts.key:
Meaning: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means that f(x) can be made as close to L as desired by taking x sufficiently close to a, while keeping x ≠ a. Look for the connection between closeness of x to a and closeness of f(x) to L, with agreement from both sides when both sides are in the domain. Common slips: saying x must equal a or that f(a) must equal L.

Example sketch: draw y = x + 1 for x ≠ 2, with an open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot at (2, 5). Supporting sentence: As x approaches 2 from either side, x + 1 approaches 3, while the filled dot gives f(2) = 5.

Accept any function whose values approach 3 from both sides of 2 and whose value at 2 is 5. Look for correctly placed open and filled dots and a sentence explaining nearby values. Common slip: drawing a branch that approaches 5 near x = 2.

handouts.title: Velocity of an object dropped on the Moon
handouts.usedIn: Velocity of an object dropped on the Moon

blocks.text: An object is dropped on the Moon. After t seconds it has fallen s(t) = 0.81t² meters. Work alone.

blocks.hint: Find s(4), in meters.
Find the average velocity over [4, 4.1], with your working.
Find the average velocity over [4, 4.01], with your working.
Estimate the velocity at t = 4, with units.

handouts.key:
s(4) = 0.81(4²) = 12.96 m.

Over [4, 4.1]: s(4.1) = 0.81(16.81) = 13.6161 m. Average velocity = (13.6161 − 12.96)/0.1 = 6.561 m/s.

Over [4, 4.01]: s(4.01) = 0.81(16.0801) = 13.024881 m. Average velocity = (13.024881 − 12.96)/0.01 = 6.4881 m/s.

Estimated velocity at t = 4: 6.48 m/s downward. For h ≠ 0, (s(4 + h) − s(4))/h = (6.48h + 0.81h²)/h = 6.48 + 0.81h, which approaches 6.48 as h approaches 0.

Look for position differences divided by time differences and units of m/s. Common slips: dividing by 4.1 or 4.01, or reporting the distance 12.96 m as a velocity.

blocks.text: Use the table to estimate lim x→0 of (sin x)/x. Here x is in radians.

blocks.caption: Values of (sin x)/x, rounded to five decimal places

blocks.hint: Your estimate of the limit.
One sentence saying what in the table supports your estimate.

handouts.key:
Estimated limit: 1.

Supporting sentence: As x approaches 0 from either side, the table values approach 1.

Look for evidence from both negative and positive x. The entries 1.00000 are rounded: at x = ±0.001, the value is approximately 0.9999998333. Common slips: treating the rounded entries as exact equality or concluding that the limit does not exist because the expression is undefined at x = 0.

l_3d386b53a622.title: Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits
l_3d386b53a622.summary: Students compute limits algebraically with the limit laws, factoring and the Squeeze Theorem, and read one-sided and infinite limits, with a recitation quiz.
readings: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, Chapter 2 (to confirm): Calculating limits using the limit laws

segments.title: Homework in, and a limit with a hole
segments.description:
The Weekly online homework on tangent lines, velocity and the idea of a limit is due now; it was submitted online before this meeting.
Put the function from last time that was undefined at 3 on the screen.
Everyone writes the limit as x approaches 3 and one reason, alone for two minutes.
Two students say what they wrote, and the instructor asks whether it could be found without a table.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: 6, because f(x) = x + 3 for every x ≠ 3. The aim today is to get such answers exactly by algebra. Nothing is collected in class.
shown: What number does f(x) approach as x approaches 3? Can you find it without a table?

segments.title: Limit laws and direct substitution
segments.description:
State the laws for lim f(x) = L and lim g(x) = M: sum, difference, constant multiple, product, quotient (M ≠ 0), power and root. Say each one in words.
Work lim_{x→2} (3x² − 5x + 1) one law at a time.
Before the quotient law is written, students predict in one sentence why M ≠ 0 is required, and a partner checks it.
Conclude that for a polynomial, or a rational function whose denominator is not zero at a, the limit is f(a); this is direct substitution.
Students then evaluate two limits alone for three minutes, naming the law behind each step, and compare with a partner for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes:
Work: 3·4 − 10 + 1 = 3. The laws need both limits to exist.
Practice: 1. lim_{x→−1} (x³ + 2x)/(x² + 4) = −3/5. 2. lim_{x→4} (x − 1)√(2x + 1) = 9.
Tie ‘plug in’ to the laws. Watch sign slips at x = −1.
shown: If lim_{x→a} f(x) = L and lim_{x→a} g(x) = M, then lim [f(x) + g(x)] = L + M and lim [f(x)·g(x)] = L·M.

segments.title: When substitution gives 0/0: factor and cancel
segments.description:
Return to lim_{x→3} (x² − 9)/(x − 3). Substitution gives 0/0, which says nothing about the limit; call it an indeterminate form.
Factor the numerator, cancel x − 3, and note that x + 3 agrees with the original for every x ≠ 3, so the limits agree.
Students factor x² − x − 2 on paper before lim_{x→2} (x² − x − 2)/(x² − 4) is finished.
Students then work three limits alone for five minutes, first checking what substitution gives, and the instructor shows the results for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes:
Second example: (x − 2)(x + 1)/((x − 2)(x + 2)) gives 3/4. Cancelling is legal because x ≠ a in a limit.
Practice: 1. expand to 6h + h², limit 6. 2. (x − 1)/(x + 1) gives 3. 3. x³ − 1 = (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) gives 3. Hint for 3: difference of cubes.

segments.title: Radicals: multiply by the conjugate
segments.description:
Take lim_{x→0} (√(x + 4) − 2)/x, which gave about 0.25 in the table last time. Substitution gives 0/0 and nothing can be factored.
Students write the conjugate of √(x + 4) − 2 before the instructor multiplies top and bottom by it.
The numerator becomes x, which cancels, and the limit is 1/(√4 + 2) = 1/4.
Students explain to a partner why the algebra turns the table estimate into an exact value, for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Conjugate: √(x + 4) + 2. Since (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b², the numerator is (x + 4) − 4 = x. Algebra turns last time’s estimate 0.25 into exactly 1/4.

segments.title: Choose the method
segments.description:
For each limit, students choose substitution, factoring or the conjugate, write one sentence of reason, then compute. They work alone for five minutes.
Partners compare their choices and reasons for two minutes.
The instructor takes the answers and asks which choices were close calls, for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. Substitute: 3/4.
2. Factor: −6.
3. Conjugate: 1/6.
Accept either valid method with a reason.

segments.title: Three cases, three moves
segments.description:
Students tell a partner in one minute what to do when substitution gives a defined number, gives 0/0 in a rational expression, or gives 0/0 in an expression with radicals.
The instructor sums up: laws plus algebra give exact limits where tables only estimate.
Preview the next meeting: limits from the left and from the right, and a limit that tables could not settle.
segments.teacherNotes: A number: that is the limit. 0/0: factor or use the conjugate. A nonzero number over 0 is treated in the third meeting. Keep it short.

segments.title: Two sides of x = 1
segments.description:
Put the function from last time that followed y = x + 1 for x < 1 and sat at 3 for x ≥ 1 on the screen.
Students write the number the values approach from the left and from the right, alone for two minutes, then compare with a neighbor for one minute.
Introduce the notation lim_{x→1⁻} f(x) and lim_{x→1⁺} f(x) and record both values.
segments.teacherNotes: Left: 2. Right: 3. Last time the conclusion was that the limit does not exist; now it gets a precise reason. The signs name the side of approach, not the sign of the number.
shown: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 1; f(x) = 3 for x ≥ 1
What number do the values of f approach as x approaches 1 from the left? From the right?

segments.title: One-sided limits and when a limit exists
segments.description:
Define the left-hand and right-hand limits. State the theorem: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L exactly when both one-sided limits equal L.
Recall h(x) = |x|/x from last time: left −1, right 1, so no limit.
Show piecewise functions A and B. Students decide which has a two-sided limit before any values are computed, then compute both sides.
Students then work three limits alone for six minutes, finding the one-sided limits first, and compare with a partner for one minute.
segments.teacherNotes:
A: left 5, right 5, limit 5. B: left 5, right 6, no limit. Common error: letting the value at the point decide.
Practice: 1. left −1, right 1, no limit. 2. 0. 3. both sides 3, limit 3. Hint for 1: rewrite |x − 4| on each side.
shown: A: f(x) = 3x − 1 for x < 2; f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≥ 2. Find lim_{x→2} f(x).
B: g(x) = x + 4 for x < 1; g(x) = 7 − x² for x ≥ 1. Find lim_{x→1} g(x).
Practice 3. k(x) = 2x + 5 for x < −1; k(x) = x² + 2 for x ≥ −1. Find lim_{x→−1} k(x).

segments.title: The Squeeze Theorem and x² sin(1/x)
segments.description:
State the theorem: if f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) near a (except possibly at a) and lim f = lim h = L, then lim g = L.
Raise lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x). The product law fails because sin(1/x) has no limit at 0, as sin(π/x) had none last time.
Write −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1. Students multiply by x² to find the two bounding functions.
The instructor shows the graph trapped between y = x² and y = −x², and both bounds go to 0.
segments.teacherNotes: Bounds: −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x². Multiplying by x² ≥ 0 keeps the direction of the inequalities. The squeeze needs the same limit on both sides; the factor x² forces the oscillation to die.

segments.title: Squeeze three limits
segments.description:
Students write the bounds and the limit for each item alone for seven minutes.
Partners swap papers and check that each step uses the theorem correctly, for two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. −x⁴ ≤ x⁴ cos(2/x) ≤ x⁴, limit 0.
2. −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x|, limit 0.
3. (x² − 4x + 7) − (4x − 9) = (x − 4)² ≥ 0, and both bounds equal 7 at x = 4, so the limit is 7.

segments.title: True or false, with a reason
segments.description:
Pairs decide whether each of three statements is true or false and write a one-line reason or counterexample, for three minutes.
The class votes by show of hands on each statement, for one minute.
One pair defends its answer on a statement where the class disagrees, and the class judges it, for two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes:
1. False: f(2) may differ or be undefined.
2. True.
3. True, by the squeeze.
Push for a concrete function in statement 1, such as a function with an open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot elsewhere. If the class agrees on all three, ask one pair to defend statement 1.
shown: 1. If lim_{x→2⁻} f(x) = 3 and lim_{x→2⁺} f(x) = 3, then f(2) = 3.
2. If lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, then both one-sided limits at a exist and are equal.
3. If −x² ≤ g(x) ≤ x² for all x, then lim_{x→0} g(x) = 0.

segments.title: Sides and squeezes
segments.description:
The instructor summarizes: check both sides when the rule changes at a point, and trap a wiggly function between two simple ones.
Preview the next meeting: what happens when values grow without bound near a point.
segments.teacherNotes: One-sided limits are the key to absolute values and piecewise rules, which return when continuity is studied later in the course.

segments.title: What happens to 1/x² near 0
segments.description:
Show a table of f(x) = 1/x² at x = ±0.1 and ±0.01.
Students predict f(0.001) and f(−0.001) alone for two minutes and say what the pattern suggests, then compare with a partner for one minute.
Reveal the values and ask what number they approach.
segments.teacherNotes: f(0.001) = 1,000,000 and f(−0.001) = 1,000,000. No number: the values grow without bound. Good answers say ‘it keeps getting larger’.

segments.title: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
segments.description:
Define lim_{x→a} f(x) = ∞: the values of f can be made as large as we like by taking x close enough to a, x ≠ a. Write lim_{x→0} 1/x² = ∞ and define −∞ the same way.
Say that ∞ is not a number, so the limit does not exist as a real number, and the notation tells us why.
Students predict the sign of 1/x as x → 0⁻ before the one-sided limits of 1/x are written.
Define a vertical asymptote x = a as a line where a one-sided limit is ∞ or −∞.
Students then find four limits alone for five minutes, writing the sign of the denominator, and compare with a partner for two minutes.
segments.teacherNotes:
Right of 0 gives ∞; left gives −∞, so lim_{x→0} 1/x does not exist. Contrast 1/x² (∞ both sides) with 1/x. Draw both graphs.
Practice: 1. ∞. 2. −∞. 3. ∞. 4. does not exist. Common error: writing ∞ for item 4.

segments.title: Sign analysis for rational functions
segments.description:
Take g(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x² − 9). Factor to (x − 3)(x + 2)/((x − 3)(x + 3)) and cancel: at 3 there is a hole with limit 5/6, not an asymptote.
At x = −3 the reduced form (x + 2)/(x + 3) has numerator near −1 and denominator near 0.
Students predict the sign of (x + 2)/(x + 3) as x → −3⁻ before the instructor shows it, then the right side follows.
State the rule for these rational functions: on each side, a numerator tending to a nonzero number divided by a denominator tending to 0 with a fixed sign gives ∞ or −∞. Determine the sign from the signs of the pieces, then compare the two sides.
Students then factor the denominator of k(x), list the candidate lines and find the one-sided limits at each alone for five minutes. The instructor shows a sign table for one minute.

x → −3⁻: (−1)/(0⁻) = ∞. x → −3⁺: −∞. So x = −3 is an asymptote and x = 3 a hole.

keyIdeas: The limit laws let us build the limit of a sum, product, quotient, power or root from the limits of simpler pieces. Direct substitution gives the limit of a polynomial, or of a rational function whose denominator is not zero at a.

When substitution gives 0/0, rewrite the expression by factoring or multiplying by a conjugate. The new expression equals the old one for x ≠ a, so it has the same limit, and the answer is exact where a table only estimates.
A two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal. The value f(a) never decides it.
The Squeeze Theorem: if g is trapped between two functions with the same limit L at a, then g has limit L. It settles x² sin(1/x), where the product law cannot be used.
An infinite limit describes values growing without bound, not a number. Where one occurs the graph has a vertical asymptote, and the sign of each factor decides between ∞ and −∞.

vocabulary.definition: Finding a limit by evaluating the function at a, valid for polynomials and for rational functions whose denominator is not zero at a.
An expression such as 0/0 that substitution produces; it tells nothing about the limit until the expression is rewritten.
For a − b, the expression a + b. Multiplying by it removes a square root, since (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b².
The limit as x approaches a from the left (x → a⁻) or from the right (x → a⁺) only.
If f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) near a and f and h both have limit L at a, then g has limit L at a.
The notation lim f(x) = ∞ (or −∞) means f(x) grows without bound, positive (or negative), as x approaches a.
A line x = a near which a one-sided limit of f is ∞ or −∞.

study.overview: This lesson turned limits from estimates read off a table into exact answers. The limit laws let you build a limit from simpler pieces. Algebra handles the cases where substitution fails. One-sided limits decide whether a two-sided limit exists. The Squeeze Theorem handles oscillating functions. Infinite limits describe values that grow without bound and mark vertical asymptotes. Reading for this material is Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, Chapter 2 (to confirm), the section on calculating limits using the limit laws.

points.heading: Substitution, and what to do when it gives 0/0
points.explanation:
Suppose lim f(x) = L and lim g(x) = M as x → a. Then the limit of a sum, difference, constant multiple, product, power or root is built from L and M in the obvious way. The limit of a quotient is L/M only when M ≠ 0. For a polynomial, or a rational function whose denominator is not zero at a, the limit is f(a). For example, lim_{x→2} (3x² − 5x + 1) = 3·4 − 10 + 1 = 3.

If substitution gives 0/0, the form is indeterminate: it tells you nothing yet. Rewrite the expression. Take lim_{x→3} (x² − 9)/(x − 3). Factor the numerator to get (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3). For x ≠ 3 this equals x + 3, and a limit never uses the value at x = 3 itself. So the limit is 3 + 3 = 6. This is why cancelling is legal, and it is why the answer is exact.

With radicals, nothing factors, so multiply by the conjugate. Take lim_{x→0} (√(x + 4) − 2)/x. Multiply top and bottom by √(x + 4) + 2. The numerator becomes (x + 4) − 4 = x, which cancels the x below. What remains is 1/(√(x + 4) + 2), whose limit is 1/(√4 + 2) = 1/4. A table gives only about 0.25. The algebra gives exactly 1/4.

Decision rule: if substitution gives a number, that is the limit. If it gives 0/0 in a rational expression, factor. If it gives 0/0 with radicals, use the conjugate.

points.heading: One-sided limits and when a two-sided limit exists
points.explanation:
The left-hand limit lim_{x→a⁻} f(x) uses only x < a. The right-hand limit lim_{x→a⁺} f(x) uses only x > a. The signs name the side of approach, not the sign of the number. The key theorem: lim_{x→a} f(x) = L exactly when both one-sided limits exist and equal L. The value f(a) never decides the question.

Example A: f(x) = 3x − 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² + 1 for x ≥ 2. From the left, 3·2 − 1 = 5. From the right, 2² + 1 = 5. The two sides agree, so lim_{x→2} f(x) = 5.

Example B: g(x) = x + 4 for x < 1 and g(x) = 7 − x² for x ≥ 1. From the left, 1 + 4 = 5. From the right, 7 − 1 = 6. The sides differ, so lim_{x→1} g(x) does not exist, even though g(1) = 6 is defined.

The same idea explains h(x) = |x|/x at 0. For x < 0 it equals −1, and for x > 0 it equals 1, so there is no limit. Whenever the rule changes at the point, or an absolute value appears, find both one-sided limits first.

points.heading: The Squeeze Theorem
points.explanation:
If f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) near a (except possibly at a), and lim f = lim h = L, then lim g = L. Both bounds must have the same limit.

This settles lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x). The product law cannot be used, because sin(1/x) oscillates wildly near 0 and has no limit there. Instead, start with −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 for x ≠ 0. Multiply every part by x². Since x² ≥ 0, the inequalities keep their direction:

−x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x².

Both −x² and x² tend to 0 as x → 0, so lim_{x→0} x² sin(1/x) = 0. The graph is trapped between y = x² and y = −x², and the factor x² forces the oscillation to die out.

Check the sign of whatever you multiply by. If the factor can be negative, as x can be, the inequalities reverse. In that case use |x| for the bound instead.

points.heading: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
points.explanation:
The statement lim_{x→a} f(x) = ∞ means the values of f can be made as large as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a. The symbol ∞ is not a number, so such a limit does not exist as a real number. The notation tells us why it fails. The definition of −∞ is the same with large negative values. A vertical asymptote x = a is a line where a one-sided limit is ∞ or −∞.

Two contrasts. For f(x) = 1/x², we get f(±0.1) = 100 and f(±0.01) = 10,000. The values grow without bound on both sides, so lim_{x→0} 1/x² = ∞. For 1/x, the right side gives ∞ and the left side gives −∞. The two-sided limit does not exist, and writing ∞ for it is a common error.

To decide the sign, look at each factor. Take g(x) = (x² − x − 6)/(x² − 9) = (x − 3)(x + 2)/((x − 3)(x + 3)). For x ≠ 3 this equals (x + 2)/(x + 3). At x = 3 the limit is 5/6, so there is a hole and no asymptote. Near x = −3 the numerator is close to −1 and the denominator is close to 0. As x → −3⁻, the denominator is a small negative number, so (−1)/(0⁻) gives ∞. As x → −3⁺, the denominator is a small positive number, so the limit is −∞. Therefore x = −3 is a vertical asymptote.

handouts.key:
1. Method: substitution. The denominator approaches 4, which is nonzero, so the quotient law applies. lim_{x→1} (x + 2)/(x + 3) = (1 + 2)/(1 + 3) = 3/4. Look for a reason that identifies the nonzero denominator.

2. Method: factoring. Substitution gives 0/0, so simplify before evaluating. x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3). For x ≠ −3, (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = x − 3. Therefore, the limit is −3 − 3 = −6. Look for cancellation of the factor x + 3. Common slip: treating 0/0 as the limit.

3. Method: the conjugate. Substitution gives 0/0, and multiplying by √(x + 9) + 3 removes the radical difference. For x ≠ 0, (√(x + 9) − 3)/x = ((x + 9) − 9)/(x(√(x + 9) + 3)) = 1/(√(x + 9) + 3). The limit is 1/(3 + 3) = 1/6. Common slip: multiplying only the numerator by the conjugate.

handouts.key:
1. Since −1 ≤ cos(2/x) ≤ 1 and x⁴ ≥ 0, −x⁴ ≤ x⁴ cos(2/x) ≤ x⁴ for x ≠ 0. Both bounding functions approach 0 as x → 0. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim_{x→0} x⁴ cos(2/x) = 0. Common slip: using the product law when cos(2/x) has no limit.

2. Since |sin(1/x)| ≤ 1, |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x|. Thus −|x| ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ |x| for x ≠ 0. Both bounds approach 0 as x → 0. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim_{x→0} x sin(1/x) = 0. Look for bounds valid on both sides of 0. Common slip: writing −x ≤ x sin(1/x) ≤ x for negative x without reversing the inequalities.

3. The lower bounding function is 4x − 9; the upper bounding function is x² − 4x + 7. At x = 4, the lower bound is 16 − 9 = 7, and the upper bound is 16 − 16 + 7 = 7. Both are polynomials, so both limits equal 7. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim_{x→4} g(x) = 7. Look for both bound evaluations and the theorem in the conclusion.

handouts.title: Factor, cancel and conjugate

blocks.text: Try each limit before the solution is worked on the board. Do the first two in pairs and the last two alone. Show your steps.
Pairs: lim_{x→4} (x² − 16)/(x² − 3x − 4)

blocks.hint: Check what substitution gives, then simplify.

blocks.text: Pairs: lim_{x→−1} (x² + 3x + 2)/(x² − 1)

blocks.hint: Check what substitution gives, then simplify.
Show the conjugate you use and the simplified expression.
Combine the fractions in the numerator first, then simplify.

handouts.key:
1. Substitution gives 0/0. Factor: x² − 16 = (x − 4)(x + 4) and x² − 3x − 4 = (x − 4)(x + 1). For x ≠ 4 near 4, the quotient equals (x + 4)/(x + 1). The limit is (4 + 4)/(4 + 1) = 8/5. Common slip: canceling individual terms rather than common factors.

2. Substitution gives 0/0. Factor: x² + 3x + 2 = (x + 1)(x + 2) and x² − 1 = (x + 1)(x − 1). For x ≠ −1 near −1, the quotient equals (x + 2)/(x − 1). The limit is (−1 + 2)/(−1 − 1) = −1/2. Common slip: losing the negative sign in the denominator.

3. Substitution gives 0/0. Use the conjugate √x + 5. For x ≠ 25, (√x − 5)/(x − 25) = (x − 25)/((x − 25)(√x + 5)) = 1/(√x + 5). The limit is 1/(5 + 5) = 1/10. Look for multiplication of both numerator and denominator by the conjugate.

4. Combine the numerator: 1/(x + 2) − 1/2 = (2 − (x + 2))/(2(x + 2)) = −x/(2(x + 2)). For x ≠ 0 near 0, dividing by x gives −1/(2(x + 2)). The limit is −1/(2·2) = −1/4. Common slip: simplifying 2 − (x + 2) to x instead of −x.

handouts.title: One-sided limits and squeeze

blocks.text: Work alone. For each problem, write the one-sided limits or the inequality you use, then your conclusion.
Let f(x) = 2kx − 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = x² + 6 for x ≥ 1. Find the value of k for which lim_{x→1} f(x) exists.

blocks.hint: Left-hand limit, right-hand limit, then k.

blocks.text: Does lim_{x→−1} |x + 1|/(x² − 1) exist? Give a reason using one-sided limits.

blocks.hint: Rewrite |x + 1| on each side of −1, then find both one-sided limits.

blocks.text: Find lim_{x→0} x² cos(5/x).

blocks.hint: Write the bounds and the limit.

blocks.text: A function g satisfies 3x ≤ g(x) ≤ x³ + 2 for all x near 1. Find lim_{x→1} g(x).

blocks.hint: Evaluate both bounds at x = 1, then state the limit.

handouts.key:
1. The left-hand limit at 1 is 2k − 1. The right-hand limit is 1² + 6 = 7. A two-sided limit exists when 2k − 1 = 7, so 2k = 8 and k = 4. The resulting limit is 7. Look for equality of the one-sided limits as the reason for choosing k.

2. For x > −1, |x + 1| = x + 1, so |x + 1|/(x² − 1) = 1/(x − 1) near −1. The right-hand limit is 1/(−1 − 1) = −1/2. For x < −1, |x + 1| = −(x + 1), so the quotient equals −1/(x − 1). The left-hand limit is −1/(−1 − 1) = 1/2. The two-sided limit does not exist because the one-sided limits differ. Common slip: using |x + 1| = x + 1 on both sides.

3. Since −1 ≤ cos(5/x) ≤ 1 and x² ≥ 0, −x² ≤ x² cos(5/x) ≤ x² for x ≠ 0. Both bounds approach 0. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim_{x→0} x² cos(5/x) = 0. Look for the bounding inequality and the common limit of the bounds.

4. At x = 1, the lower bound 3x equals 3, and the upper bound x³ + 2 equals 1 + 2 = 3. Both polynomial bounds approach 3 as x → 1. By the Squeeze Theorem, lim_{x→1} g(x) = 3. The bounds are ordered near 1 because x³ + 2 − 3x = (x − 1)²(x + 2) ≥ 0 there.

handouts.title: Infinite limits

blocks.text: Work alone. For each limit, write the sign of the numerator and of the denominator near the point, then the limit (∞, −∞ or does not exist). Name any vertical asymptote.

blocks.hint: Signs of the pieces, the limit, and the asymptote.

blocks.text: lim_{x→0} (x − 3)/x²

blocks.hint: Signs of the pieces, the limit, and the asymptote.

handouts.key:
1. The numerator is 3, which is positive. As x → 1⁺, the denominator x − 1 is positive and approaches 0. Thus lim_{x→1⁺} 3/(x − 1) = ∞. The vertical asymptote is x = 1. Look for the positive denominator on the specified side.

2. Near 0, the numerator x − 3 is negative and approaches −3. For x ≠ 0, the denominator x² is positive and approaches 0 from above on both sides. Thus lim_{x→0} (x − 3)/x² = −∞. The vertical asymptote is x = 0. Common slip: reporting ∞ without accounting for the negative numerator.

t_eed4f36c45d5.prompt: A speedometer reads 80 mph at 2:15 pm. Speed is distance divided by time, and an instant lasts no time. What does the speedometer reading mean?
followUps: One answer says the car would cover 80 miles if it held this speed for an hour. Another says it is the car’s speed over a very short window around 2:15. Can both be right, and how do they differ?
Suppose you measured the car’s average speed over one minute, then over one second, then over a hundredth of a second. What would you expect to happen to those numbers?
Why can’t we find the speed at 2:15 by dividing the distance traveled in zero time by zero?

t_db0ce1298ba1.prompt: Suppose a classmate fills in a table for f(x) = sin(π/x) at x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and sees 0 every time, so claims that the limit as x approaches 0 is 0. Another student uses x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13 and gets 1 every time, so claims the limit is 1. Who is right, and what would you need to see before trusting an estimate of a limit from a table?
followUps: Both tables have x values that get closer and closer to 0. What does that tell you about whether the values of sin(π/x) settle toward one number?
For g(x) = (x − 1)/(x² − 1) near x = 1, the table behaved well. What is different about the values in that table compared with the sin(π/x) tables?
How could a graph of sin(π/x) near 0 help you decide, and what would you look for?

t_c20f78f83a4a.prompt: For r(x) = (x² − 25)/(x − 5), a table gives r(4.9) = 9.9, r(4.99) = 9.99, r(5.01) = 10.01 and r(5.1) = 10.1. What is the best estimate of lim_{x→5} r(x)?
t_c20f78f83a4a.explanation: The values approach 10 as x approaches 5 from both sides. “5” confuses the input approached with the output approached; “0” treats the undefined quotient 0/0 as zero; “The limit does not exist.” confuses r(5) being undefined with nearby values failing to approach a number.

t_b66984cdad2a.prompt: The graph of p follows the line y = 3x − 2 except at x = 2. It has an open circle at (2, 4) and a filled dot at (2, 7). What are lim_{x→2} p(x) and p(2), respectively?
t_b66984cdad2a.explanation: Nearby points on the line approach height 4, while the filled dot gives p(2) = 7. “7 and 4” reverses the limit and the function value; “4 and 4” uses the open circle as the function value; “7 and 7” uses the filled dot to decide the limit.

t_e6db08f7c247.prompt: Which statement correctly explains lim_{x→−2} f(x) = 6?

choices.text: f(x) must equal 6 whenever x is sufficiently close to −2, with x ≠ −2.
f(−2) must equal 6, regardless of the values of f(x) at nearby inputs.
f(x) can be made as close to −2 as desired by taking x sufficiently close to 6, with x ≠ 6.
f(x) can be made as close to 6 as desired by taking x sufficiently close to −2, with x ≠ −2.

t_e6db08f7c247.explanation: The limit describes outputs near 6 for inputs sufficiently close to −2 but different from −2. “f(x) must equal 6 whenever x is sufficiently close to −2, with x ≠ −2.” replaces closeness with exact equality; “f(−2) must equal 6, regardless of the values of f(x) at nearby inputs.” substitutes the value at the point for nearby behavior; “f(x) can be made as close to −2 as desired by taking x sufficiently close to 6, with x ≠ 6.” interchanges the input and output.

t_fd137260d2a6.prompt: If q(x) = x + 4 for x ≠ 3 and q(3) = −1, then lim_{x→3} q(x) = 7.
t_fd137260d2a6.explanation: For inputs near 3 but different from 3, q(x) = x + 4 approaches 7 from both sides. The assigned value q(3) = −1 does not change that limit.

t_e29b4ea5d956.prompt: Suppose a falling object’s downward displacement is s(t) = 5t² meters after t seconds. Average velocity over [3, 3 + h] is (s(3 + h) − s(3))/h. A student substitutes h = 0 and writes: “The quotient is 0/0, so the instantaneous velocity at t = 3 is 0 m/s.” Identify the mistake. Calculate the average velocities for h = 0.1 and h = 0.01, then use them to estimate the instantaneous velocity.
t_e29b4ea5d956.answer: 0/0 is undefined, not zero. For h ≠ 0, the average velocity is 30 + 5h m/s. It is 30.5 m/s when h = 0.1 and 30.05 m/s when h = 0.01. These values approach 30 m/s, so the estimated instantaneous velocity is 30 m/s downward.
t_e29b4ea5d956.explanation: Expanding gives s(3 + h) − s(3) = 5(9 + 6h + h²) − 45 = 30h + 5h². Dividing by h for h ≠ 0 gives 30 + 5h. Substituting the two nonzero interval lengths gives 30.5 and 30.05 m/s. Instantaneous velocity is the number these average velocities approach as the interval shrinks, rather than the result of substituting h = 0 into the original quotient.

t_010d606b37ad.title: Weekly online homework: Tangent lines, velocity and the idea of a limit
t_010d606b37ad.prompt: Complete this assignment as your own work. Submit it online before the first meeting of the next lesson, “Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits.” It contributes to Weekly online homework (15% of the course grade). Your work is scored individually using the rubric below: three criteria, each worth up to 4 points, for a total of 12 points. Show calculations, explain your estimates and label units where appropriate. For review, use Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, sections 2.1 and 2.2 (to confirm). A secant slope is (change in y)/(change in x). Average velocity is (change in position)/(change in time). The statement lim_{x→a} f(x) = L means that f(x) can be made as close to L as we like by taking x close enough to a, with x ≠ a.
steps: For the curve y = x³ and the point P(2, 8), calculate the secant slope (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) at x = 1.9, 1.99, 2.01 and 2.1. Organize your results in a table. Estimate the tangent slope at P, explain how both sides support your estimate and write the estimated tangent line using y − 8 = m(x − 2).

Suppose a falling object’s downward displacement is modeled by d(t) = 4.8t² meters after t seconds. Calculate its average velocity over [4, 4.1], [4, 4.01] and [3.99, 4]. Estimate its instantaneous velocity at t = 4, including units. Explain why shrinking the time interval helps and why substituting an interval length of zero does not give a velocity.

For F(x) = (x³ + 1)/(x + 1), the table gives F(−1.1) = 3.31, F(−1.01) = 3.0301, F(−0.99) = 2.9701 and F(−0.9) = 2.71. Estimate lim_{x→−1} F(x). Explain what the values on each side support, whether F(−1) is defined and why this table supports an estimate rather than proving the limit.

A graph follows y = x² + 2 for every x except x = −2. It has an open circle at (−2, 6) and a filled dot at (−2, 0). Sketch the graph near x = −2. State lim_{x→−2} H(x) and H(−2), where H names the graphed function. Explain why these answers differ.

Explain in your own words what lim_{x→−3} K(x) = 2 means. Construct and sketch a function K whose limit at −3 is 2 but whose value K(−3) is −4. Give a formula or a precise graph description, label the open circle and filled dot, and explain how nearby values support the limit.
t_010d606b37ad.answerKey:
1. For x ≠ 2, (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) = x² + 2x + 4. The slopes at x = 1.9, 1.99, 2.01 and 2.1 are 11.41, 11.9401, 12.0601 and 12.61. Values from below and above 2 approach 12, so the estimated tangent slope is 12. The tangent line is y − 8 = 12(x − 2), or y = 12x − 16.
2. d(4) = 76.8 m, d(4.1) = 80.688 m, d(4.01) = 77.18448 m and d(3.99) = 76.41648 m. Average velocities are (80.688 − 76.8)/0.1 = 38.88 m/s, (77.18448 − 76.8)/0.01 = 38.448 m/s and (76.8 − 76.41648)/0.01 = 38.352 m/s. The estimated instantaneous velocity is 38.4 m/s downward. Shorter intervals give average velocities closer to this number from either side. A zero interval length produces 0/0, which is undefined.
3. The estimated limit is 3. As x approaches −1 from below, the listed values decrease toward 3; from above, they increase toward 3. F(−1) is undefined because its formula gives 0/0. A finite table shows only selected inputs, so it supports an estimate without establishing behavior at every sufficiently close input.
4. The sketch follows the parabola y = x² + 2 near −2, with an open circle at (−2, 6) and a filled dot at (−2, 0). The limit is 6 and H(−2) = 0. Nearby graph values approach 6 from both sides, while the filled dot assigns the value at −2.
5. Accept wording that says K(x) can be made arbitrarily close to 2 by taking x sufficiently close to −3, with x ≠ −3. One valid construction is K(x) = x + 5 for x ≠ −3 and K(−3) = −4. Sketch the line y = x + 5 with an open circle at (−3, 2) and a filled dot at (−3, −4). Nearby values of x + 5 approach 2 from both sides, while the filled dot sets K(−3) = −4. Other correctly justified constructions are valid.

t_56206199f476.prompt: Is this statement true or false? If lim_{x→2⁻} f(x) = 3 and lim_{x→2⁺} f(x) = 3, then f(2) = 3. Decide with your partner and write a one-line reason or a counterexample.
followUps: Can you sketch a function with an open circle at (2, 3) and a filled dot somewhere else on the line x = 2 that makes the statement fail? What does this graph say about the two-sided limit at 2?
Statement 2 says: if lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, then both one-sided limits at a exist and are equal. How is that different from statement 1, and which direction does the limit theorem actually run?
Statement 3 says: if −x² ≤ g(x) ≤ x² for all x, then lim_{x→0} g(x) = 0. Could g wiggle wildly near 0 and still have this limit? What does the squeeze need on both sides?

t_77c3f01b63ac.prompt: A classmate says lim_{x→0} 1/x = ∞, because 1/x gets enormous when x is close to 0. Do you agree? What happens to 1/x on each side of 0, and how does that compare with 1/x²?
followUps: Which sign does 1/x take for x slightly greater than 0, and which for x slightly less than 0? What does each one-sided limit say about the graph near x = 0?
Why does 1/x² give ∞ from both sides while 1/x does not? What in the denominator makes the difference?
Is ∞ a number? When we write lim_{x→0} 1/x² = ∞, what are we saying about the values of f, and what does the line x = 0 do on the graph?

t_59d48bd28355.explanation: Factor to obtain (x − 3)(x + 3)/((x + 2)(x + 3)). For x ≠ −3, cancel x + 3. The limit is (−3 − 3)/(−3 + 2) = 6. “−6” loses the negative sign in the denominator. “0” uses the numerator’s limit without checking the denominator. “The limit does not exist.” mistakes the indeterminate form 0/0 for a conclusion.

t_3e45a9910dab.explanation: Multiply numerator and denominator by √(x + 16) + 4. For x ≠ 0, the expression becomes 1/(√(x + 16) + 4), whose limit is 1/8. “1/4” omits the added 4 in the denominator. “0” treats the numerator’s limit as the quotient’s limit. “8” gives the denominator’s limit instead of its reciprocal.

t_943dfb979435.prompt: Let p(x) = 2x + 7 for x < −2, p(−2) = 9, and p(x) = x² − 1 for x > −2. The two-sided limit of p(x) as x approaches −2 does not exist.
t_943dfb979435.explanation: The left-hand limit is 2(−2) + 7 = 3. The right-hand limit is (−2)² − 1 = 3. Both equal 3, so the two-sided limit exists and equals 3. The value p(−2) = 9 does not determine the limit.

t_8b9c02c96efe.prompt: Which conclusion about lim_{x→0} x² sin(3/x) is justified?

choices.text: It does not exist because sin(3/x) has no limit.
It equals 0 because −x² ≤ x² sin(3/x) ≤ x².

t_8b9c02c96efe.explanation: Since −1 ≤ sin(3/x) ≤ 1 and x² ≥ 0, multiplying gives the stated bounds. Both bounds approach 0, so the Squeeze Theorem gives limit 0. “It equals 1 because sin(3/x) ≤ 1.” treats an upper bound as the limit. “It equals −1 because sin(3/x) ≥ −1.” treats a lower bound as the limit. “It does not exist because sin(3/x) has no limit.” overlooks that multiplication by x² can force the product toward 0.

t_985ebb42f1e6.prompt: A student writes −x ≤ x sin(2/x) ≤ x for every x ≠ 0 and uses these bounds to conclude that lim_{x→0} x sin(2/x) = 0. Identify the error, give bounds valid on both sides of 0, and explain whether the conclusion is correct.
t_985ebb42f1e6.answer: The proposed inequalities fail for x < 0 because multiplying by a negative number reverses the inequalities. Valid bounds are −|x| ≤ x sin(2/x) ≤ |x|. Both bounds approach 0, so the conclusion is correct by the Squeeze Theorem.
t_985ebb42f1e6.explanation: Start with −1 ≤ sin(2/x) ≤ 1. For x > 0, multiplication gives −x ≤ x sin(2/x) ≤ x. For x < 0, it gives x ≤ x sin(2/x) ≤ −x. These combine as −|x| ≤ x sin(2/x) ≤ |x|. The student’s conclusion is correct, but the original bounds do not justify it on both sides of 0.

t_2f6c22cdb310.title: Weekly recitation quizzes: Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits
t_2f6c22cdb310.prompt: Time allowed: 15 minutes. This paper counts toward Weekly recitation quizzes (15%) and is marked in points. Follow the instructor’s announcement about what you may bring or use. Show the algebra, one-sided limits, inequalities or sign analysis requested. Give exact answers.
steps:
Evaluate each limit. For (a), name the limit law that permits substitution. For (b) and (c), show your algebraic simplification.
(a) lim_{x→2} (x³ − 1)/(x² + 2)
(b) lim_{x→5} (x² − 25)/(x² − 3x − 10)
(c) lim_{x→0} (√(x + 36) − 6)/x (8 points)

Let r(x) = 2x − 2 for x < 3, r(3) = 20, and r(x) = x + 2 for x > 3. Find lim_{x→3⁻} r(x) and lim_{x→3⁺} r(x). Use these values to decide whether lim_{x→3} r(x) exists, and explain your conclusion. (3 points)
Evaluate lim_{x→0} x³ cos(1/x). Write lower and upper bounds valid on both sides of 0. Explain how the Squeeze Theorem gives your answer. (3 points)
Evaluate lim_{x→1⁻} (x + 4)/(x − 1)². State the signs of the numerator and denominator near 1 on the indicated side. Explain the infinite limit and name the vertical asymptote. (3 points)
t_2f6c22cdb310.answerKey:
1. (a) 7/6. The quotient law applies because the denominator tends to 6 ≠ 0. Award 1 point for the quotient law with its nonzero-denominator condition and 1 point for 7/6.
(b) Factor to (x − 5)(x + 5)/((x − 5)(x + 2)). For x ≠ 5 near 5, this equals (x + 5)/(x + 2), so the limit is 10/7. Award 1 point for correct factorization, 1 point for cancellation valid away from 5, and 1 point for 10/7.
(c) Multiply numerator and denominator by √(x + 36) + 6. The numerator becomes x, giving 1/(√(x + 36) + 6) for x ≠ 0. The limit is 1/12. Award 1 point for multiplication by the conjugate, 1 point for the simplified expression, and 1 point for 1/12. (8 points)
2. The left-hand limit is 2·3 − 2 = 4. The right-hand limit is 3 + 2 = 5. The two-sided limit does not exist because the one-sided limits differ. Award 1 point for 4, 1 point for 5, and 1 point for the conclusion supported by their inequality. (3 points)
3. Since |cos(1/x)| ≤ 1, −|x|³ ≤ x³ cos(1/x) ≤ |x|³ for x ≠ 0. Both bounding functions tend to 0 as x → 0. The Squeeze Theorem therefore gives a limit of 0. Award 1 point for valid bounds on both sides, 1 point for the common limit of the bounds, and 1 point for the conclusion using the Squeeze Theorem. (3 points)
4. The numerator is positive and tends to 5. The denominator is positive and tends to 0. Thus the quotient grows without bound, so the limit is ∞ and x = 1 is a vertical asymptote. Award 1 point for both signs, 1 point for ∞ explained by a positive numerator tending to 5 divided by a positive denominator tending to 0, and 1 point for x = 1. (3 points)
Total: 17 points

t_029c78283af9.title: Weekly online homework: Limit laws, one-sided limits and infinite limits
t_029c78283af9.prompt: Complete this assignment as your own work. Submit it online before the first meeting of the next lesson, “Continuity, the Intermediate Value Theorem and limits at infinity.” It contributes to Weekly online homework (15% of the course grade). Your work is scored individually using the rubric below: three criteria, each worth up to 4 points, for a total of 12 points. Show calculations and explain why each method applies. Give exact answers for finite limits. For review, use Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, Chapter 2 (to confirm), Calculating limits using the limit laws.
steps: Evaluate each limit. For the first, name the limit laws that justify substitution. For the others, state what substitution gives and show the algebraic simplification: lim_{x→3} (x³ + 2)/(x² + 4); lim_{x→−4} (x² + 3x − 4)/(x² + 6x + 8); lim_{x→9} (√(x + 7) − 4)/(x − 9). Explain why simplifying an expression for x ≠ a preserves its limit as x approaches a.

Let q(x) = kx + 1 for x < −3, q(−3) = 11, and q(x) = x² − 2 for x > −3. Find the value of k for which lim_{x→−3} q(x) exists. Show both one-sided limits and state the two-sided limit for that value of k. Explain whether changing q(−3) would change your answer.

Evaluate lim_{x→0} x²(2 + cos(3/x)). Begin with −1 ≤ cos(3/x) ≤ 1 for x ≠ 0. Construct lower and upper bounds valid on both sides of 0. Find their limits and explain how the Squeeze Theorem applies. Explain why the product law alone does not justify the result.

Let v(x) = (x² + 7x + 10)/(x² + 2x − 15). Factor and simplify v(x), stating where the simplified expression agrees with the original. Find lim_{x→−5} v(x), lim_{x→3⁻} v(x), and lim_{x→3⁺} v(x). Explain the signs near 3. Classify the behavior at x = −5 and x = 3 as a hole or a vertical asymptote, and explain whether a two-sided limit at 3 exists as a real number.
t_029c78283af9.answerKey:
1. The power, sum, and quotient laws give (3³ + 2)/(3² + 4) = 29/13; the denominator tends to 13 ≠ 0. For the second limit, substitution gives 0/0. Factor to (x + 4)(x − 1)/((x + 4)(x + 2)); for x ≠ −4 near −4, this equals (x − 1)/(x + 2), so the limit is (−5)/(−2) = 5/2. For the radical limit, substitution gives 0/0. Multiply by (√(x + 7) + 4)/(√(x + 7) + 4) to obtain (x − 9)/((x − 9)(√(x + 7) + 4)). For x ≠ 9, this equals 1/(√(x + 7) + 4), whose limit is 1/8. Limits depend on values near the approach point, so equality there preserves the limit.
2. The left-hand limit is −3k + 1. The right-hand limit is 9 − 2 = 7. Equality requires −3k + 1 = 7, hence k = −2. Both one-sided limits then equal 7, so the two-sided limit is 7. Changing q(−3) does not affect either one-sided limit or their equality.
3. Adding 2 gives 1 ≤ 2 + cos(3/x) ≤ 3. Since x² ≥ 0, multiplication gives x² ≤ x²(2 + cos(3/x)) ≤ 3x². Both bounds tend to 0, so the Squeeze Theorem gives a limit of 0. The product law alone does not apply because 2 + cos(3/x) has no limit as x approaches 0.
4. v(x) = (x + 5)(x + 2)/((x + 5)(x − 3)). The original domain excludes −5 and 3; on that domain, v(x) = (x + 2)/(x − 3). Thus lim_{x→−5} v(x) = (−3)/(−8) = 3/8, giving a hole at (−5, 3/8). Near 3, the numerator approaches 5 and is positive. From the left, the denominator approaches 0 through negative values, so lim_{x→3⁻} v(x) = −∞. From the right, it approaches 0 through positive values, so lim_{x→3⁺} v(x) = ∞. The line x = 3 is a vertical asymptote. The two-sided limit at 3 does not exist as a real number.

f_2f93a49cc81a.question: Why can’t I find the velocity at t = 5 by putting h = 0 into the average velocity formula?
f_2f93a49cc81a.answer: Putting h = 0 into (s(5 + h) − s(5))/h gives 0/0, which is undefined. It is not 0 and it tells you nothing. An instant has no length, so the formula cannot be used at h = 0. For any h ≠ 0 the quotient simplifies. With s(t) = 4.9t² it becomes 49 + 4.9h. As h gets smaller, these values approach 49, so the velocity at t = 5 is 49 m/s. The limit describes where the values are heading, not what happens at h = 0.

f_2334c7cbf238.question: If the value f(a) plays no role, why does a limit at a make sense when f(a) is undefined?
f_2334c7cbf238.answer: A limit only looks at values of f(x) for x near a but not equal to a. Take f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3). It is undefined at x = 3 because it gives 0/0. For x ≠ 3 it equals x + 3, so f(2.99) = 5.99 and f(3.01) = 6.01. The values head toward 6, so the limit at 3 is 6. Even when f(3) exists, it can differ from the limit, because the limit does not use it.

f_fa52a1f5e99f.question: How do I know my estimate from a table or graph is right?
f_fa52a1f5e99f.answer: A table or graph gives an estimate, not a proof. Check values from both sides of a. If the left and right values approach different numbers, the limit does not exist. Also be careful about how you choose the inputs. For f(x) = sin(π/x), the values at x = 1, 1/2, 1/3, … are all 0. The values at x = 2/5, 2/9, 2/13, … are all 1. Both lists get as close to 0 as you like, so the outputs never settle. Look at more than one pattern of inputs and at the graph before you trust a guess. Later in the course, limit laws will let you confirm such estimates exactly.

f_4b0d7a083a34.question: In lim_{x→3} (x² − 9)/(x − 3), I cancel x − 3, but x − 3 is zero at x = 3. Why is that allowed?
f_4b0d7a083a34.answer: A limit only looks at values of x near 3, never at x = 3 itself. For every x ≠ 3, (x² − 9)/(x − 3) = (x − 3)(x + 3)/(x − 3) = x + 3. The two expressions agree at every point the limit examines, so they have the same limit, which is 6. The cancelled expression is not equal to the original at x = 3, where the original is undefined. That does not matter for the limit.

f_67fd6ff796e3.question: If the left-hand and right-hand limits are both 3, does f(2) have to be 3? And what if the value at the point is different from the one-sided limits?
f_67fd6ff796e3.answer: No. The two-sided limit at a exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal, and then the limit is that common value. The value f(a) plays no part. It can be a different number, or f(a) can be undefined, and the limit is unchanged. Likewise, if f(x) = x + 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = 3 for x ≥ 1, the value f(1) = 3 matches the right-hand limit. But the left-hand limit is 2, so the two-sided limit does not exist. Always compute both sides before deciding.

f_4b33967effb5.question: Why can’t I use the product law on x² sin(1/x) as x → 0, and why does the Squeeze Theorem work instead?
f_4b33967effb5.answer: The product law requires both factors to have limits. The factor x² has limit 0, but sin(1/x) oscillates between −1 and 1 infinitely often near 0 and has no limit. So the law does not apply. The Squeeze Theorem avoids the problem. Since −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 and x² ≥ 0, multiplying gives −x² ≤ x² sin(1/x) ≤ x² for x ≠ 0. Both bounds tend to 0, so the trapped function also tends to 0. Check the sign of the factor you multiply by. A negative factor, as in x sin(1/x), reverses the inequalities, so use |x| as the bound instead.
